assessment.prompt: Five new questions revisit the week’s events, interpretations, and source distinctions. Taking the assessment completes the week; missed answers remain practice priorities.

question.prompt: Why does Theseus choose the bandit-ridden land road to Athens instead of the safe sea voyage?

choices.text: He wants to win renown through deeds, imitating Heracles — arriving having done something worth remembering
He cannot pay for a ship
The sea route is blocked by storms
He wants to avoid recognition

question.explanation: Theseus refuses the safer way deliberately: a hero should earn his arrival, as Heracles cleared monsters.

question.prompt: What pattern unites Theseus's victories over the road bandits?

choices.text: He spares each bandit after winning surrender
He turns each bandit's own cruelty back on them — club, bent pines, cliff, and bed
He traps each bandit in a labyrinth
Each duel is won by divine intervention

question.explanation: Plutarch notes Theseus imitated Heracles by returning on assailants the same violence they dealt.

question.prompt: How does Aegeus save Theseus from Medea's poisoned cup?

choices.text: Medea confesses before Theseus drinks
A servant switches the cups
He recognizes the sword Theseus draws at dinner — the token he left under the rock — and knocks the cup away
An oracle warns him at the table

question.explanation: Theseus draws his sword 'as if he designed to cut with it'; Aegeus recognizes the token and throws down the cup.

question.prompt: How does Theseus escape the labyrinth after killing the Minotaur?

choices.text: He memorizes Daedalus's floor plan
The Minotaur's dying cry opens the walls
Ariadne leads him out by hand
He follows Ariadne's thread — tied at the entrance and unwound through the maze — back out

question.explanation: Ariadne gives him a clue (ball) of thread; he unwinds it through the windings and follows it out.

question.prompt: Why does King Aegeus die at Theseus's homecoming?

choices.text: The crew forgets to raise the white sail; seeing black sails, Aegeus believes his son dead and throws himself down
Medea poisons him before fleeing Athens
The Minotaur's curse reaches him
He dies of old age while Theseus is at sea

question.explanation: The forgotten sail signal costs Aegeus his life — and names the Aegean Sea.

assessment.title: Achilles and the Iliad assessment
assessment.prompt: Five new questions revisit the week’s events, interpretations, and source distinctions. Taking the assessment completes the week; missed answers remain practice priorities.

question.prompt: What triggers Apollo's plague on the Greek camp at the Iliad's opening?

choices.text: Achilles refuses to fight the Trojans
Agamemnon refuses and mocks the priest Chryses, who came to ransom his daughter Chryseis
The Greeks steal Apollo's golden tripod
Chryses poisons the wells

question.explanation: Chryses came to ransom his daughter; the king's insult brought Apollo's arrows on the host.

question.prompt: After Briseis is taken, what does Achilles ask his mother Thetis to win from Zeus?

choices.text: That Agamemnon be struck by lightning
That he be made king of the army
That the Trojans prevail — so the Greeks suffer until they learn what Achilles was worth
That his ships be spared for the voyage home

question.explanation: Achilles asks Zeus to favour the Trojans; the army's suffering will prove his worth — and nearly destroys it.

question.prompt: Why does Achilles reject Agamemnon's enormous offer of gifts in Iliad 9?

choices.text: The offer arrives too late; he has already sailed
He demands the kingship, not gifts
He has sworn an oath to Hector
The stripped honour is beyond material compensation — he will fight only when fire reaches his own ships

question.explanation: Achilles refuses everything; no list of tripods and gold can repair the public insult to his honour.

question.prompt: What sequence leads to Patroclus being killed at Troy?

choices.text: Wearing Achilles's armour, he presses past the warning to Troy's walls, where Apollo and Hector kill him
Defending the ships as they burn
In single combat with Aeneas
Caught in an ambush returning to camp

question.explanation: Patroclus ignores the warning, chases to the walls, and dies to Apollo and Hector — redirecting Achilles's rage.

question.prompt: Why does Achilles release Hector to Priam after dragging the body for days?

choices.text: Zeus orders it directly
Priam kneels and asks him to think of his own father, Peleus — the two enemies weep together
The ransom gold outweighs his rage
The Greek commanders demand it

question.explanation: Shared grief breaks the rage: Priam's plea for his son's body recalls Achilles's own father.

question.prompt: How does Penelope hold off the suitors for three years?

choices.text: She feigns illness in a locked tower
She makes them sail to Delphi first
She weaves a burial shroud by day and unravels it by night
She marries one in secret

question.explanation: The loom trick is undone only by a servant's betrayal.

question.prompt: What does the Cyclops episode cost Odysseus?

choices.text: He loses his best crewmen to the Cyclops's club
His ship is wrecked on the island's rocks
He is trapped for seven years
His boast gives Polyphemus his name — Poseidon's curse ensures the voyage home is slow and solitary

question.explanation: Outis saves him; the boast curses him — every later trial rides on Poseidon's anger.

question.prompt: What lets Odysseus hear the Sirens' song and survive?

choices.text: He plugs his crew's ears and has himself bound to the mast — engineering helplessness in advance
He memorises a counter-song from Circe
He kills the Sirens before passing
He steers by their island at night

question.explanation: The Sirens teach pre-commitment: the only safe exposure to a fatal lure is arranged while you are still rational.

question.prompt: What do the dead reveal about the price of glory?

choices.text: They demand gold before speaking
Achilles would trade his fame for a poor man's life — the dead measure what the living pay for renown
They reveal only the way through Scylla
They tell him his crew is doomed by hubris alone

question.explanation: Anticleia died of longing; Achilles prefers labour to lordship of the dead.

question.prompt: How does Penelope prove the beggar is Odysseus?

choices.text: She checks the scar on his thigh
She asks about the Trojan Horse
She tests him with the bed — it is rooted to a living olive tree, a secret only he could know
She watches him defeat the suitors

question.explanation: The immovable bed is the recognition the epic saves for last.

question.prompt: What triggers the quest for the Golden Fleece?

choices.text: The oracle commands a fleece offering
Jason seeks glory to win a bride
The Argonauts are hired for a trading voyage
Pelias, warned by an oracle of a one-sandalled man, sends Jason on a quest meant to kill him

question.explanation: The quest is Pelias's trap, not Jason's ambition.

question.prompt: What must Jason do to earn the fleece from Aeetes?

choices.text: Yoke fire-breathing bulls and sow dragon's teeth that rise as armed men
Kill the Colchian champion in single combat
Solve the riddle of the dragon grove
Bring a tribute of gold to the king

question.explanation: The tasks are impossible by design — and the king intends betrayal either way.

question.prompt: What is the decisive factor in winning the fleece?

choices.text: Jason's superior strength at the tasks
Medea's aid — her ointment, her trick, her calming of the dragon — at the price of betraying her father
Aeetes's honourable bargain
The Argonauts' night assault

question.explanation: Every winning move is Medea's; Jason's feat depends on her choice.

question.prompt: What marks the flight from Colchis?

choices.text: A storm sent by Zeus
A mutiny among the Argonauts
Apsyrtus's death and a pursuit that requires purification before the voyage can continue
The loss of the fleece overboard

question.explanation: The brother's killing is the flight's defining crime; the escape is bought with kin-blood.

question.prompt: How does Euripides' Medea end?

choices.text: She is executed by Creon's soldiers
She returns the fleece to Colchis
She sails into exile alone
She destroys Jason with a poisoned robe and the killing of their sons, then escapes to Athens — where she later poisons Theseus's cup

question.explanation: Her refuge at Aegeus's court links straight back to week 1's poisoned-cup scene.

assessment.title: Heracles assessment
assessment.prompt: Five new questions revisit the week’s events, interpretations, and source distinctions. Taking the assessment completes the week; missed answers remain practice priorities.

question.prompt: What event sentences Heracles to twelve years of labours?

choices.text: He killed his children in Hera-sent madness — the oracle sentences him to serve Eurystheus
He wants to win the throne of Tiryns
Eurystheus hires him as a mercenary
He seeks the gods' favour for a quest

question.explanation: The labours are penance, not ambition — the darkest origin for the greatest hero.

question.prompt: How does Heracles overcome the Nemean lion's unbreakable hide?

choices.text: He beheads it with his nephew Iolaus at his side
He strangles it barehanded, then skins it with its own claws — the trophy becomes his signature garb
He starves it in its cave
He blinds it and ties it up

question.explanation: The lionskin and club that identify him in every image start with this fight.

question.prompt: What drives the persecution of Heracles?

choices.text: Eurystheus's envy of his strength
A curse on his father Amphitryon
Hera's hatred of Zeus's mortal-born son — it produces the madness, the kin-killing, and the sentence of service
His refusal of divine honours

question.explanation: The whole labour-cycle flows from Hera's jealousy — she is the engine of his suffering.

question.prompt: How does Heracles die, and what follows?

choices.text: He falls at Hades’ gate in Library 2.5.2
He is killed by Eurystheus's soldiers
He dies old and forgotten
A poisoned robe from Deianira (the centaur's revenge) — then pyre on Oeta and ascent to Olympus, the only deified hero

question.explanation: His end is unique: mortality burned away, divinity ascended.

question.prompt: What makes Heracles dangerous to allies as well as monsters?

choices.text: The same strength that clears monsters also breaks cities and hospitality — the myths preserve both halves
He is only dangerous when drunk
He refuses all labours but easy ones
He serves the wrong king

question.explanation: He is the honest hero: the power that protects is the power that wrecks.

assessment.prompt: Five new questions revisit the week’s events, interpretations, and source distinctions. Taking the assessment completes the week; missed answers remain practice priorities.

question.prompt: What sets Perseus's story in motion?

choices.text: Danae's secret marriage to a rival king
An oracle that Acrisius's grandson will kill him — so he seals Danae away, Zeus arrives as gold, and mother and infant are cast to sea
A famine that empties Argos
Polydectes's invasion of Argos

question.explanation: The prophecy creates the conditions it predicts — the classic pattern.

question.prompt: How is Perseus manoeuvred into the Gorgon quest?

choices.text: A drunken boast at a feast
A challenge from the oracle
Polydectes's 'wedding contribution' scam — Perseus can't offer a horse and rashly promises anything; the king names Medusa's head
A ransom for his mother's freedom

question.explanation: The errand is engineered to remove the son guarding the mother.

question.prompt: What is the key technique of the Gorgon kill?

choices.text: He creeps up on her in total darkness
He uses the cap of invisibility to approach awake
He poisons her food
He watches only the reflection in Athena's mirrored shield while striking the sleeping Medusa

question.explanation: The mirrored shield is the answer to 'how do you kill what kills you by sight?'

question.prompt: Why is Andromeda chained to the sea-cliff?

choices.text: Her mother Cassiopeia's boast against the sea-nymphs — Poseidon sends flood and monster, and the oracle names the princess
She refused the god's advances
Her father's gambling debt
She is punished for stealing fire

question.explanation: The innocent daughter pays for the mother's pride — a recurring formula.

question.prompt: How does the prophecy about Acrisius come true?

choices.text: Deliberately — Perseus kills him on returning to Argos
Accidentally — at funeral games, Perseus's discus swerves and kills his grandfather among the spectators
In the palace when the Gorgon head is shown
By poison from Medusa's head

question.explanation: Fate completes itself on a stray discus — the oracle never misses.

assessment.title: Heroes on Stage assessment
assessment.prompt: Five new questions revisit the week’s events, interpretations, and source distinctions. Taking the assessment completes the week; missed answers remain practice priorities.

question.prompt: What is the deepest motive behind Agamemnon's murder?

choices.text: Aegisthus's ambition for the throne
A quarrel over Trojan spoils
Clytemnestra's revenge for Iphigenia — the daughter sacrificed to launch the fleet
Apollo's command for justice

question.explanation: The sacrifice at Aulis is the wound; the carpet and the bath are only the staging.

question.prompt: How does the Oresteia resolve the blood-feud?

choices.text: Orestes is purified at Delphi and pardoned
The Furies are destroyed by Zeus
Orestes kills himself to end the cycle
Athena establishes a court at the Areopagus — law replaces vendetta, and the Furies are honoured, not defeated

question.explanation: Aeschylus's answer to endless retaliation is an institution.

question.prompt: What is Antigone's core argument against Creon?

choices.text: Divine law and burial duty outrank a king's decree — the unwritten laws of the gods are older than the state
Polynices was the rightful king
Creon has no legal right to rule
The burial was ordered by the oracle

question.explanation: She appeals above the state to the gods — which is why the conflict cannot be settled politically.

question.prompt: What is the twist at the heart of Oedipus Rex?

choices.text: Tiresias is the murderer
The detective is the murderer — the king who hunts Laius's killer finds himself
Laius faked his death
The Sphinx set a trap for Oedipus

question.explanation: The play inverts every mystery: self-discovery is the catastrophe.

question.prompt: What does The Trojan Women show that the Iliad does not?

choices.text: The gods' political manoeuvres
Achilles's heroism
The defeated side's price — enslaved queens and a murdered child, the cost side of the same victory
The siege tactics of Troy

question.explanation: Euripides prices the same war the Iliad glorifies — for an audience that was itself an empire.

assessment.title: Afterlives of Heroes assessment
assessment.prompt: Five new questions revisit the week’s events, interpretations, and source distinctions. Taking the assessment completes the week; missed answers remain practice priorities.

question.prompt: What does the Persephone myth explain?

choices.text: The creation of the first humans
The origin of the Eleusinian Mysteries' secrets only
The founding of Athens
The seasons — her descent and return as a grieving mother's cycle, sealed by the pomegranate seeds

question.explanation: The custody arrangement is the weather — and the promise that descent isn't the end.

question.prompt: What did hero cults mean in real Greek life?

choices.text: Tombs as active shrines, cities claiming heroes' bones, and myths treated as early history rather than fiction
A secret religion for initiates
A literary club for reading Homer
Worship forbidden by the city-states

question.explanation: Heroes were part of civic religion — the stories were their past, not just stories.

question.prompt: Why does Ovid matter to how we know Greek myth?

choices.text: He translated the Iliad into Latin
His Roman re-telling preserved many tales in their best-known form — Narcissus, Pyramus and Thisbe, Arachne, Icarus
He invented all the transformation myths
He was the original source of every tale

question.explanation: Much 'Greek mythology' in art and literature is Ovid's polished version.

question.prompt: How is myth written into the physical world?

choices.text: Only in written maps
Through temple dedications alone
The Aegean Sea for Aegeus, constellations for Perseus's rescue, the Pillars of Hercules, and cities claiming founders
Via names of months

question.explanation: The landscape is the memory — names of seas and stars keep the stories physical.

question.prompt: Which hero model does what?

choices.text: All four are models of strength
Only Achilles and Odysseus matter
They represent the same archetype
Achilles is glory-at-cost, Odysseus cunning endurance, Theseus civic founding, Heracles labour and apotheosis

question.explanation: The arc's final question: which kind of strength does the world need?

An oracle that Acrisius's grandson will kill him — so he seals Danae away, Zeus arrives as gold, and mother and infant are cast to sea
A famine that empties Argos
Polydectes's invasion of Argos

question.explanation: The prophecy creates the conditions it predicts — the classic pattern.

question.prompt: How is Perseus manoeuvred into the Gorgon quest?

choices.text: A drunken boast at a feast
A challenge from the oracle
Polydectes's 'wedding contribution' scam — Perseus can't offer a horse and rashly promises anything; the king names Medusa's head
A ransom for his mother's freedom

question.explanation: The errand is engineered to remove the son guarding the mother.

question.prompt: What is the key technique of the Gorgon kill?

choices.text: He creeps up on her in total darkness
He uses the cap of invisibility to approach awake
He poisons her food
He watches only the reflection in Athena's mirrored shield while striking the sleeping Medusa

question.explanation: The mirrored shield is the answer to 'how do you kill what kills you by sight?'

question.prompt: Why is Andromeda chained to the sea-cliff?

choices.text: Her mother Cassiopeia's boast against the sea-nymphs — Poseidon sends flood and monster, and the oracle names the princess
She refused the god's advances
Her father's gambling debt
She is punished for stealing fire

question.explanation: The innocent daughter pays for the mother's pride — a recurring formula.

question.prompt: How does the prophecy about Acrisius come true?

choices.text: Deliberately — Perseus kills him on returning to Argos
Accidentally — at funeral games, Perseus's discus swerves and kills his grandfather among the spectators
In the palace when the Gorgon head is shown
By poison from Medusa's head

question.explanation: Fate completes itself on a stray discus — the oracle never misses.

question.prompt: What is the deepest motive behind Agamemnon's murder?

choices.text: Aegisthus's ambition for the throne
A quarrel over Trojan spoils
Clytemnestra's revenge for Iphigenia — the daughter sacrificed to launch the fleet
Apollo's command for justice

question.explanation: The sacrifice at Aulis is the wound; the carpet and the bath are only the staging.

question.prompt: How does the Oresteia resolve the blood-feud?

choices.text: Orestes is purified at Delphi and pardoned
The Furies are destroyed by Zeus
Orestes kills himself to end the cycle
Athena establishes a court at the Areopagus — law replaces vendetta, and the Furies are honoured, not defeated

question.explanation: Aeschylus's answer to endless retaliation is an institution.

question.prompt: What is Antigone's core argument against Creon?

choices.text: Divine law and burial duty outrank a king's decree — the unwritten laws of the gods are older than the state
Polynices was the rightful king
Creon has no legal right to rule
The burial was ordered by the oracle

question.explanation: She appeals above the state to the gods — which is why the conflict cannot be settled politically.

question.prompt: What is the twist at the heart of Oedipus Rex?

choices.text: Tiresias is the murderer
The detective is the murderer — the king who hunts Laius's killer finds himself
Laius faked his death
The Sphinx set a trap for Oedipus

question.explanation: The play inverts every mystery: self-discovery is the catastrophe.

question.prompt: What does The Trojan Women show that the Iliad does not?

choices.text: The gods' political manoeuvres
Achilles's heroism
The defeated side's price — enslaved queens and a murdered child, the cost side of the same victory
The siege tactics of Troy

question.explanation: Euripides prices the same war the Iliad glorifies — for an audience that was itself an empire.

assessment.prompt: Five new questions revisit the week’s events, interpretations, and source distinctions. Taking the assessment completes the week; missed answers remain practice priorities.

question.prompt: What does the Persephone myth explain?

choices.text: The creation of the first humans
The origin of the Eleusinian Mysteries' secrets only
The founding of Athens
The seasons — her descent and return as a grieving mother's cycle, sealed by the pomegranate seeds

question.explanation: The custody arrangement is the weather — and the promise that descent isn't the end.

question.prompt: What did hero cults mean in real Greek life?

choices.text: Tombs as active shrines, cities claiming heroes' bones, and myths treated as early history rather than fiction
A secret religion for initiates
A literary club for reading Homer
Worship forbidden by the city-states

question.explanation: Heroes were part of civic religion — the stories were their past, not just stories.

question.prompt: Why does Ovid matter to how we know Greek myth?

choices.text: He translated the Iliad into Latin
His Roman re-telling preserved many tales in their best-known form — Narcissus, Pyramus and Thisbe, Arachne, Icarus
He invented all the transformation myths
He was the original source of every tale

question.explanation: Much 'Greek mythology' in art and literature is Ovid's polished version.

question.prompt: How is myth written into the physical world?

choices.text: Only in written maps
Through temple dedications alone
The Aegean Sea for Aegeus, constellations for Perseus's rescue, the Pillars of Hercules, and cities claiming founders
Via names of months

question.explanation: The landscape is the memory — names of seas and stars keep the stories physical.

question.prompt: Which hero model does what?

choices.text: All four are models of strength
Only Achilles and Odysseus matter
They represent the same archetype
Achilles is glory-at-cost, Odysseus cunning endurance, Theseus civic founding, Heracles labour and apotheosis

question.explanation: The arc's final question: which kind of strength does the world need?
